title: Number of Strings Which Can Be Rearranged to Contain Substring
statement:
Call a string *good* when it is made only of lowercase English letters and its letters can be put in some order so that `"leet"` shows up as a contiguous piece of the result. For example, `"lteer"` is good (it can become `"leetr"`), while `"letl"` is not.

Given an integer `n`, count how many different good strings have length exactly `n`. The count can be huge, so return it modulo `10^9 + 7`.
notes:
## Intuition

Reordering is free, so only the letter counts matter: a string is good exactly when it has at least one `l`, at least one `t` and at least two `e`s. Counting the good strings directly is awkward, but counting the **bad** ones is easy, because each way of being bad is a simple condition:

- A: no `l` (25^n strings), B: no `t` (25^n), C: at most one `e` (25^n with no `e` plus n·25^(n-1) with exactly one).

Inclusion-exclusion gives |A ∪ B ∪ C| from the sizes of the sets and their overlaps, and the answer is 26^n minus that. A letter-by-letter DP over (has `l`, has `t`, number of `e`s up to 2) also works in O(n); the formula needs only a few fast powers.

## Approach

1. Work in `BigInt` with `MOD = 10^9 + 7`, and write `power` as fast exponentiation by squaring.
2. `all = 26^n` counts every string.
3. `singles = |A| + |B| + |C| = 3·25^n + n·25^(n-1)`.
4. `pairs = |A∩B| + |A∩C| + |B∩C| = 24^n + 2(24^n + n·24^(n-1))`: two letters are banned (or limited).
5. `triples = |A∩B∩C| = 23^n + n·23^(n-1)`.
6. `good = all - singles + pairs - triples`; bring it back into `[0, MOD)` and return it as a number.

## Example 1, step by step

For `n = 4` nothing reaches the modulus: `all = 456976`, `singles = 1171875 + 62500 = 1234375`, `pairs = 995328 + 110592 = 1105920`, `triples = 279841 + 48668 = 328509`. Then `456976 - 1234375 + 1105920 - 328509 = 12`: the 12 orderings of l, e, e, t.

## Complexity

- Time: O(log n): a handful of fast powers.
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- Products of two residues reach about 10^18, past what a JavaScript number holds exactly; use `BigInt` (or split the multiplication).
- After subtracting, `good` can be negative modulo `MOD`; add `MOD` before the final `%`.
- C is "at most one `e`", not "no `e`": forgetting the n·25^(n-1) strings with a single `e` overcounts.
- For `n < 4` the answer is 0; the formula gives that on its own.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `MOD`, `len` | the modulus and `n` as `BigInt`s |
| `power` | fast modular exponentiation |
| `all` | number of strings of length `n` |
| `singles`, `pairs`, `triples` | inclusion-exclusion sums over one, two and three bad conditions |
| `good` | strings that meet all three conditions |

narration.2: Work with BigInt so products of two large residues stay exact.
narration.7: Keep going while bits of the exponent remain.
narration.8: The lowest bit is 1, so this power of the base is part of the result.
narration.11: Square the base for the next bit of the exponent.
narration.12: Drop the lowest bit of the exponent.
narration.17: Every string of length n: 26 choices per position.
narration.18: Strings with no l, plus no t, plus at most one e.
narration.19: Overlaps of two conditions: no l and no t, and each of those with at most one e.
narration.20: Strings breaking all three: no l, no t and at most one e.
narration.21: Inclusion-exclusion removes every bad string exactly once.
narration.22: Bring the result into [0, MOD) and return it as a plain number.
